name: Bardi
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bardi is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Katsika (2008) 'Acoustic Correlates of Primary Stress in Bardi', is an unpublished Yale term paper (Glottolog 317101, from Bowern's bibliography): no copy exists online (checked Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex, Katsika's 2023 CV, Bowern's site), so it was not read; priority medium. Its findings are reported second-hand by Bowern, McDonough & Kelliher (2012, JIPA Illustration, bronze OA) and Bowern (2012, A Grammar of Bardi §3.5.1, p. 110, snippets only): primary stress falls regularly on the initial syllable of every word, stressed vowels are longer, with intensity and sometimes pitch increases; secondary stress is weight- and morphology-conditioned. Best first-hand statement read: the JIPA illustration p. 343 (saved). Also checked and silent: Metcalfe 1975 (PL B-30, full text), Bird 1910 (Anthropos 5, scanned from archive.org), Bowern & Cram LSA 2024 poster. Bowern 2002 (MITWPL 42) snippet says primary stress 'usually' initial with secondary stress on non-final odd syllables (print only). searching was done via web lookups, curl, Google Books volumes feed, Crossref, Unpaywall and archive.org.

new_statements.quote: Bardi is analyzed as having a stress system. By stress we mean relative syllable prominence. Bardi stress is not a lexical pitch accent system. Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word. Stressed vowels are characterized by increased duration compared to unstressed vowels (see Katsika 2008), though there is also a phonemic distinction in length in both stressed and unstressed syllables. [...] While primary stress is predictable and regular, the rules for secondary stress are complex and are sensitive to morphological structure and syllable weight.
new_statements.citation: Bowern, Claire, Joyce McDonough & Katherine Kelliher. 2012. Bardi. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(3): 333-351. doi:10.1017/S0025100312000217
new_statements.locator: p. 343, section 'Prosodic features' > 'Stress' (secondary-stress detail continues pp. 343-345; intonation pp. 345-347)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., JIPA 42/3, doi:10.1017/S0025100312000217, Cambridge download stamp on every page). The quoted passage is at p. 343 (PDF page 11; running header 'Claire Bowern, Joyce McDonough Katherine Kelliher: Bardi 343'), section 'Prosodic features' > 'Stress', and matches layer and a fresh extracted text of that page word for word: 'Bardi is analyzed as having a stress system. By stress we mean relative syllable prominence. Bardi stress is not a lexical pitch accent system. Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word. Stressed vowels are characterized by increased duration compared to unstressed vowels (see Katsika 2008), though there i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of every (phonological) word, regardless of syllable weight; it is demarcative, never contrastive. The grammar (2012: 110, snippet) adds that all phonological words, including pronouns, preverbs, adverbs and non-clitic conjunctions, receive this initial primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is sensitive to morphology and syllable weight (light = open syllable with short vowel; coda or long vowel = heavy). Verbs carry stress on the first syllable of the root (prefixed nouns do not); heavy case markers (-nim ERG, -ngan ALL), monosyllabic heavy clitics (=jin, =min) and agreement clitics take secondary stress, with speaker variation when a clitic follows a case marker (stress both, only the last, or only the first). In morphologically simple words: disyllables and underlyingly trisyllabic words have only the initial primary stress; trisyllables derived by final-vowel deletion stress the (heavy) third syllable; tetrasyllables stress the third syllable if the fourth is light, the fourth if heavy; further secondary stresses on final heavy syllables or otherwise the penult, then alternating left to right. Morphologically assigned stress can override the alternation and produce stress clash (pp. 343-345).
new_statements.exceptions: None for primary stress ('regular', 'consistently'); the grammar snippet says all previous detailed analyses agree, and Wikipedia's paraphrase of Bowern 2012: 110-112 adds that loanwords are also stressed initially and that stress never distinguishes minimal pairs. Speaker variation is noted only for secondary stress on case-marker + clitic sequences.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word), based on ~220 h of recordings of fluent speakers, including casual speech and storytelling. Intonation interacts: the first H* pitch accent aligns to the primary-stressed (initial) syllable of the first content word of the utterance, with downstepped !H* on later primary-stressed syllables; the grammar (2012: 110 snippet) states that at the phrase level word stress may be subordinated to intonational-phrase accent.
new_statements.identity_note: The JIPA illustration and Bowern's grammar describe Bardi as spoken at One Arm Point (Ardiyooloon) and Sunday Island descendants, Dampier Peninsula, WA -- i.e. glottocode bard1255 proper. Jawi (jawi1240, Sunday Island variety) is treated by Bowern as closely related/near-identical but is not the object of the stress description. Bird 1910's 'Chowie' (= Jawi) is a distinct older record with no stress remark.

new_statements.quote: Bardi is analyzed as having a stress system. By stress we mean relative syllable prominence. Bardi stress is not a lexical pitch accent system. Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word. Stressed vowels are characterized by increased duration compared to unstressed vowels (see Katsika 2008), though there is also a phonemic distinction in length in both stressed and unstressed syllables. In stressed syllables there are also increases in intensity and, in some cases, pitch, likely related to the intonational system.
new_statements.citation: Bowern, Claire, Joyce McDonough & Katherine Kelliher (2012). Bardi. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(3): 333-351. doi:10.1017/S0025100312000217
new_statements.locator: p. 343, 'Prosodic features' > 'Stress' (pdf page 11 of 19); secondary-stress rules continue to p. 344
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-initial primary stress on every word (demarcative, quantity-insensitive for primary stress); secondary stress is morphologically and weight-conditioned (verb-root-initial syllable; heavy case markers and clitics; third syllable of trisyllables; third or fourth of tetrasyllables depending on weight). Catalog coding for a new record would be fixed initial stress. This is the same author's statement as in the reference grammar (Bowern 2012: 110) and it cites the unobtainable Katsika 2008 term paper for the acoustic correlates.

sources.note: p. 343 'Stress': stress system, not lexical pitch accent; primary stress regular and consistently on the initial syllable of the word; stressed vowels longer (Katsika 2008), more intense, sometimes higher pitch; secondary stress complex, sensitive to morphology and weight (verb roots stressed on first root syllable; heavy case markers/clitics stressed); pp. 343-345 give the weight-based secondary-stress pattern; intonation H* aligns to primary stressed syllable of first content word (pp. 345-347). Publisher PDF served without login (HEAD 200 application/pdf, 2026-09-17).

sources.note: 'Stress is demarcative in Bardi. Primary stress in Bardi is always assigned to the first syllable, and all Bardi words receive this stress. In fact, primary stress even falls on the initial syllable of borrowed words... Stress alone never distinguishes between minimal pairs in Bardi.' Tertiary, paraphrasing the grammar pp. 110-112.

sources.quote: 5. Stress 5.1. Primary stress Bardi has a demarcative stress system. Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word. All previous detailed analyses of Bardi stress have noted primary stress in this position. Stressed vowels are characterized phonetically by increased length compared to unstressed vowels; see Katsika (2008). There are also increases in intensity and, in some cases, pitch, likely related to the intonational [system]. [...] All phonological words receive a primary stress. This includes pronouns, preverbs, adverbs, and non-clitic conjunctions.
sources.locator: ch. 3 §5.1 'Primary stress', p. 110 (Google Books search snippets, stitched from overlapping hits)
sources.note: The most authoritative primary description; snippets confirm 'Bardi has a demarcative stress system. Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word' and a fuller secondary-stress treatment (incl. reduplicated and borrowed words) than the JIPA illustration; would be the preferred citation for the catalog.
